explanation: Fires on the word 'engage' and its forms (engage, engaged, engagement, Engages, disengagement, unengaged), in every sense: taking part, betrothal, mechanical meshing, combat. Strongest on subword pieces of the word ('dis[eng]agement', 'Eng[ages]'). Weak or no firing elsewhere, apart from a few look-alike subwords such as 'og' or 'eng' inside names.

A mixture. It fires strongly on Python 'def' at the start of an indented method inside a class, on Java 'java.util.List/Map' imports, and on 'to' in the phrase 'as to'. It also fires on assorted subword pieces of names and technical terms (Thuy, Klobuchar, Bharadwaj, saturation/saturable, inflexibility). The pieces do not share one concept.

Fires on a word, often the first or second subword piece of a word, near the start of a clause in non-English Latin or Cyrillic text (Italian, Romanian, Portuguese, Danish, Norwegian, Russian, Estonian, Indonesian). Typical targets are function words such as 'per', 'Nu', 'no', 'não', 'să', 'una', or the opening piece of a word ('P', 'П'). Weaker on name pieces in English text. Ordinary English prose does not activate it.

No clear pattern. Strong activations land on unrelated tokens in many contexts: technical/code docs ('Step', 'conf', 'min', 'Enter', '^'), the space before page numbers in court headers, 'factors', 'reviews', 'like', 'to', URL characters. I see no consistent token or context.

Fires on physics and electrical-engineering terms for physical forces, fields and electrical/resonance properties: electrostatic, capacitance/capacitor, resonance/resonant, piezoresistive/piezoelectric, charge, superconductivity, quantum, electrodynamics. Strongest on 'static' in 'electrostatic'. Weaker on other quantitative science words (frequency, magnetic, rates). Nothing on general text.

Fires on a head noun that names a category or kind of system, usually as a modifier or as the head of a domain phrase. Examples: 'organ' (organ function, organ-limited), 'language', 'browser', 'IDE', 'fieldbus', 'Court' at the start of a court name, 'Month', 'antibiotic', 'sugar'. The examples look loosely tied to classifier-like nouns but are fairly scattered.

Fires on words inside time, distance or degree expressions, especially when a number or quantifier comes first: 'years' in '10-15 years ago', 'days ago', 'miles', 'floors', 'a year later', 'this week/morning', 'just south of', 'so fast'. Also fires on 'how' and 'a' in casual phrasing. Strongest on unit nouns after a number in a relative-time phrase.

No clear pattern. It fires on many unrelated tokens: sentence-initial discourse words ('some', 'Again', 'yes', 'Sometimes', 'for now', 'said it all') and code punctuation and identifiers ('(n', ');', '//', '.println', '_equals'). The common thread may be the end or start of a short clause, but that is vague.

A mixture. It fires on characters inside technical identifiers and version or address strings: digits and dots in IP addresses (127.0.0[.]1), part numbers (STM[3]2), sha384, file or library names. It also fires on scattered pieces of foreign names and of ordinary words. I found no single concept.

Fires on tokens inside boilerplate legal or licensing text, mainly software license headers ('compliance with the License', 'obtain a copy', 'distributed under the License is distributed', 'full copyright and license information, please') and cookie or terms notices ('you agree to'). Also fires on some code tokens (e.g. '>' in a C macro). Normal prose gives weak or no firing.

Fires on a word-initial subword piece, very often 'g'/'G' (GDI, -givers, gizmos, gallerists, GbE, Gy, GTest, golang, GParted, gke, gzip). Also fires on other short word-starting consonant pieces such as 'pr', 'fr', 'f', 'dec' when the whole word is split into several tokens. Strongest when the piece is 'G'/'g' at the start of a word.

No coherent pattern. Strong activations land on unrelated tokens: 'OF' in 'STATE OF OHIO' court captions, 'window', 'site', 'episode', 'his', 'from', '[', '.' in version numbers, '+', digits in arithmetic, Chinese text. I can't identify one shared feature.

Two jobs. First, leading indentation whitespace (spaces or tabs) at the start of a line in code, JSON or config text, and line-initial keywords such as Dockerfile 'COPY'. Second, the verb or preposition after a party in legal motion language ('Defendant moves', 'petitioned', 'moved for', 'argues'). Scattered other subword hits exist.

Fires mainly on tokens in code and lists that follow a delimiter: 'import'/'java'/'android'/'com' at the start of Java import lines, an opening quote after a colon in JS objects, a comma in argument lists, a quote-brace in a struct list. Also fires on assorted prose tokens ('to', 'inclusion', 'working', 'Art'). The code part is fairly consistent, but the prose hits are scattered.
